questions.question: What is the difference between an immutable object and an encapsulated one?
options: The immutable one has final fields without setters; the encapsulated one has private fields with setters
The encapsulated one cannot have getters
The immutable one uses public instead of private
explanations: They are not the same: one protects access, the other forbids changes.
Correct. Immutable = final fields + no setters. Encapsulated = private + setters with validation.
Both use getters to expose data.
Both use private to protect fields.

questions.question: What happens if you try to access a private attribute from another class?
explanations: The default value is not used.
Correct. Java does not allow accessing private fields outside their class. It fails to compile.

questions.question: When is it recommended to use a final (immutable) field instead of a private field with a setter?
options: When the value can change frequently
When the value should only be set in the constructor and not change afterwards
When validation is needed on every modification
When a default value is needed
explanations: Fields that change frequently need setters.
Correct. final + no setter = immutable. Ideal for IDs, dates, and instance constants.
Frequent validation requires setters, not final.
Default values do not determine whether to use final.
